title: I made an unofficial / fan remake of one of my favorite games from the 90's using AI: Fantasy Empires
author: InSilicoAwards
selftext:
I've spent about the past 4 weeks in Unreal with Claude and Astra doing a free fan remake of one of my favorite games from the 90's, Fantasy Empires. It was a strategy game set in the D&D world of Mystara. It had a very unique arcade battle mode where you took control of a unit during the siege. I updated it to a more third person over the shoulder view, re-balanced a lot of the troops using battle simulations, and reworked some of the UI to be friendly for modern gaming. All art, video, music, sound assets are AI-generated or CC0 (listed in the credits).

The video is a bit long -- it's not just gameplay -- it describes my interest in the original game and covers why I used AI specifically for the project. Primarily, this would be financially impossible to do without it (I think we estimated $0.7-$2.5 million in traditional assets and programming work would be required). **This would never exist without AI.**

**My workflow in sum:**

I used a coordinator and a lot of parallel threads to keep it organized, always asking it what was waiting on me, what we needed to wrap up before running a build. Because we were using parallel processes we had threads stage a diff in a review folder every time they were doing an edit, and a single current integrated build thread would apply any staged works, compile it, run checks, and commits, and package test builds.

Verification was mostly automated. The game has command-line modes that drive a full game end to end and capture screenshots off-screen (orders screens, battles, diplomacy, map effects), so a thread can check its own work visually before telling him it's done. There's a shared project memory where every rule gets written down, so a new thread three days later knows that test builds are never Shipping config.

Art and audio came from other tools wired into the same loop. Codex CLI and FAL generated portraits, sprites, icons and illustrations in a painted Mystara style. ElevenLabs produced the Dungeon Master voice and thousands of hero and troop lines. Claude wrote music in midi with different layers and voices to dynamically shift depending on how well you're doing in a battle (horns for victory, strings for loss, etc). We would always pilot an image or audio first before running an extensive batch for quality assurance. I'm sure I have a few six finger hands in the portraits somewhere still though. I intentionally went with a sprite style to push the more painterly aesthetic, to limit the work on the engine (I think I was rendering 10,000 unit battles at one point), and to get around having to model, rig, and animate around 30 units. I feel like the style keeps it unique and gives it a nod to 90's games like Dungeon Keeper and Daggerfall. Besides, there's a lot of light mapping you can do that works well with the flat sprite cards.

The real engine of the project was the playtest loop. I'd play a packaged test build, record it using Streamlabs, and drop the video plus notes into a working directory. That becomes a thread that writes up a plan per note, gets answers from me regarding any questions, fixes, and verifies the fix in the packaged game, not just in the editor.

**Why I chose to remake a pre-existing game?**

I've made some smaller party games over the past several months since Opus 5.5 arrived, but this is probably my most involved project, and it felt right to work with something that was built traditionally so I could have an established framework to develop off of. Besides, there are many old DOS games that deserve some love beyond just DOSBox emulation; some that need some balance or tweak to make them playable for modern tastes. Game is available here for download (you need the original of course): [https://kwe.mdscur.com/](https://kwe.mdscur.com/)

comments.author: OkShock6767
comments.body: Why not decompile the original instead? It then can be ported and improved.
